strengths: Novel and clearly articulated reframing: casting genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding is a genuinely fresh angle, and the paper convincingly maps document-understanding primitives (grounding, retrieval, span completion) onto genomic analysis workflows.

Strong empirical results across multiple settings: state-of-the-art average AUROC on DNALONGBENCH eQTL (0.852/0.867) with only 256K trainable probe parameters; best accuracy on nearly all RiceSubBench splits versus Evo-2 (7B) and LucaOne (1.8B); and a large practical efficiency win on whole-genome phenotype prediction (12.3 min vs. 5h40m for Evo-2).

Good ablation practice: the DeepSeek-OCR backbone ablation (+5.37% relative) shows the DNA-specific formulation adds value beyond the pretrained vision backbone; the 1D vs. 2D CNN controlled comparison (Appendix A) supports the layout claim; the resolution sweep (Table 7) supports the compression-efficiency claim.

Exceptional reproducibility effort: complete prompt/instruction protocols, task output contracts, hyperparameter tables for both pretraining corpora, baseline reproduction details, and metric definitions are all documented in detail.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper transparently reports weak results on T4 (Text-EM ≈ 0.13), T5 (low strict grounding accuracy), and T6 (0.06–0.10 chromosome accuracy), with thoughtful analysis of failure modes rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is largely in framing and data engineering: the model itself is a LoRA-adapted DeepSeek-OCR (SAM-Conv-CLIP-L encoder + DeepSeek-3B decoder) with a small multi-page fusion module and attention pooling. The core machinery is borrowed; a reader could see this as an application of an existing OCR system to a new domain rather than a new method.

The central efficiency claim may be partially confounded: '20× fewer effective tokens' derives from aggressive visual downsampling (patchify + 16× conv), but comparable token reduction could in principle be achieved in 1D via patching/downsampling of the sequence. The 1D-vs-2D controlled comparison uses only small custom CNNs (up to ~10M params, weak AUROC 0.55–0.65); stronger 1D baselines (transformers/state-space models at matched budget) are absent from that comparison, so the '2D layout inductive bias' claim is supported but not airtight.

Statistical rigor is limited: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests in the main tables; several eQTL gains are small (e.g., AT: 0.852 vs 0.852; AS: 0.813 vs 0.802); and RiceWGPB test sets are extremely small (21 and 26 accessions), making RMSE differences (2.952 vs 3.056) fragile evidence for the headline whole-genome claim.

Biological information content of the OCR formulation is not fully justified: since the DNA string is exactly known and cheap to render, the advantage rests entirely on the compression/layout argument; the paper does not analyze what the visual tokens preserve vs. discard (e.g., reconstruction fidelity of functional elements under the ~20× compression), which would strengthen the 'high-fidelity compression' claim.

Scaling and generality concerns: pretraining uses only 2048-bp windows rendered to pages, with mean pooling over pages for downstream embeddings; only two organisms (human, rice) are studied; no comparison against sequence models under matched pretraining compute, so the accuracy-efficiency frontier claims rest partly on cross-model comparisons with different training data pipelines.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and thought-provoking: reformulating genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding, with a well-articulated mapping between document-understanding primitives (grounding, retrieval, completion) and genomic operations (variant localization, subsequence search, missing-interval inference).

The method is described at an unusually high level of detail: task formulations T1-T6, supervision spaces, conversation schemas, rendering geometry, two-stage adaptation schedules, and full pretraining hyperparameters (Tables S15-S16) are all specified, which supports reproducibility of the pipeline.

The evaluation spans three progressively harder settings (DNALONGBENCH eQTL, cross-subspecies splice classification with a phylogeny-aware OOD gradient, whole-genome phenotype prediction), and the paper includes a direct ablation against the DeepSeek-OCR backbone (+5.37% relative on eQTL), which partially isolates the contribution of the DNA-specific formulation.
The appendix honestly reports the internals of the OCR tasks, including weak results (T5 localization, T4 completion, T6 chromosome classification), rather than hiding them entirely.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons are misleading. Table 2 frames the comparison as 'activated parameters' of the probing head (256K) against tiny baselines (HyenaDNA 1.6M, Caduceus 7.7M) and Enformer (252M), while the representation itself is extracted by a 3.4B-parameter (409M visual, 570M activated decoder) pretrained vision-language model. A fair comparison would report total/activated compute of the full representation pipeline; the '985× fewer parameters' claim is largely a framing artifact of counting only the head.

The central conceptual claim—that 2D visual layout is better aligned with sparse genomic semantics than 1D sequence processing—is not convincingly established. Rendering monospace A/C/G/T text into images is essentially a bijective re-encoding of the character stream; the claimed gains could as plausibly come from (a) the very strong pretrained DeepSeek-OCR backbone or (b) the fixed 100-token compression (which averages away detail the tasks may not need). The controlled 1D-vs-2D CNN comparison in Appendix A is weak evidence: the 1D CNN family degrades as it grows (0.649 → 0.578 AUROC), suggesting training/architecture issues rather than a fundamental limit of sequential processing, and the SimpleCNN baseline (0.528) is trivial.

No comparison against the natural competitor class: learned token-level compression methods (e.g., Megabyte, byte-latent transformers, or simply pooling k-mer tokens), which would directly test whether the vision pipeline is doing anything beyond lossy sequence compression. The 'understanding-driven compression' framing is asserted but not tested against such baselines.

Several appendix results undermine the fine-grained-capability narrative: T5 grounding collapses at strict IoU (Det-Acc 0.0046 at IoU=0.99 on HG38, with ℓ∞ error of 184 px vs. 0.39 px on T2), T4 masked completion achieves only ~0.13 exact match, and T6 chromosome classification reaches 0.062 accuracy—barely above the 1/25 random baseline. These are relegated to the appendix while the abstract emphasizes near-perfect ROI identification.

Statistical rigor is insufficient: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. The RiceWGPB test sets contain only 21 and 26 samples (Table S20), so the RMSE differences (2.952 vs. 3.056 for TGW) and the LucaOne outlier (8.817) cannot support claims of superiority; RiceSubBench accuracy (~0.59 for a 3-class task) is also low in absolute terms.

Potential pretraining–evaluation contamination is not discussed: OpticalDNA is pretrained on the full HG38 genome and on japonica rice accessions, then evaluated on genomic windows from the same genomes and the same accession databases (RiceSuperPIRdb), without chromosome-level or accession-level exclusion analysis.

The 'first' claims ('first vision-based DNA foundation model', 'first to reformulate genomic modeling as OCR') are overstated; treating DNA as image-like inputs has prior precedent in the literature, and the related-work section does not seriously engage with it.

No released code or pretrained checkpoints are mentioned, and there is no limitations section discussing the information-loss concerns, the scale imbalance with baselines, or the tiny RiceWGPB test sets.

strengths: Genuinely novel reframing: casting genomic modeling as OCR-style document understanding with rendered DNA 'documents' is a creative and unexplored direction, and the paper articulates a plausible alignment between OCR primitives (grounding, retrieval, completion) and genomic analysis workflows.

Strong empirical results across a progressive evaluation suite (DNALONGBENCH eQTL, RiceSubBench OOD generalization, RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype prediction), with consistent gains over recent baselines including much larger models (Evo-2 7B, LucaOne 1.8B).

The ablation against the DeepSeek-OCR backbone under an identical protocol (Fig. 3, Table S21, Table 5) is a well-designed controlled comparison that isolates the contribution of the DNA-specific document formulation and pretraining, rather than only showing that a big vision backbone helps.

Substantial reproducibility detail: pretraining hyperparameters (Tables S15–S16), task prompt/response protocols (Appendices B–D), bounding-box annotation construction (Appendix C), benchmark construction details (Appendix F), and baseline reproduction recipes (Appendix G) are documented thoroughly.

Honest treatment of weak spots: the appendix openly reports near-chance chromosome classification (T6), low masked-completion exact match (T4), and grounding as the bottleneck in retrieval (T5), with useful analysis rather than hiding failures.

Efficiency analysis (Table 7) and Grad-CAM interpretability (Appendix I.6) add meaningful evidence that compression is robust and that attributions concentrate around biologically meaningful splice loci.
weaknesses: The parameter-efficiency framing is potentially misleading: OpticalDNA builds on DeepSeek-OCR's pretrained SAM-Conv-CLIP-L encoder and DeepSeek-3B (MoE) decoder, inheriting large-scale natural-image/language pretraining. Headline claims ('985× fewer activated parameters', 'only 256k trainable parameters') count downstream adaptation, not the total pretraining investment, which is not directly comparable to genomics-only foundation models trained from scratch.

A controlled comparison against a compute-matched 1D sequence model with modern token compression (e.g., patch merging, hierarchical pooling on base/k-mer tokens) is missing. The 1D vs 2D CNN evidence (Appendix A, Table S2) uses small CNN families and does not rule out that a 1D model with 20× token compression would match these results, so the causal claim that 2D layout is the source of the advantage remains partially unestablished.

No statistical rigor: results are single runs with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite modest margins on some benchmarks (e.g., average AUROC differences of ~0.01–0.02 in Table 2 for some tissues).

No explicit code or model release statement is given; given the complexity of the rendering pipeline, task protocols, and rendering-dependent hyperparameters (font size, line spacing), reproducibility without code is uncertain.

Performance on two of the four claimed core primitives is weak: masked completion exact match (~0.13) and chromosome classification (~0.06–0.10, near the ~0.04 chance level for 25 classes). This undercuts the claim that the six OCR-style tasks learn 'core genomic primitives' comprehensively; reading/grounding appear strong, but retrieval and completion do not.

The rendering choice appears somewhat brittle and under-ablated: the model must learn to read a synthetic monospace font at a fixed resolution, and 2048-bp windows span ~2 pages. Why rendering is preferable to directly feeding compressed tokens to the same decoder is not convincingly isolated beyond the small-CNN study.

The efficiency claim of 'nearly 20× fewer effective tokens' is partly a tokenization/accounting choice (compression ratio ~19–21 in Table 7) rather than demonstrated wall-clock superiority over 1D baselines at matched accuracy in the main results; the strongest timing evidence (Table 4) compares against frozen Evo-2/LucaOne extractors on a specific setup.

Some limitations (e.g., 70k context cap for Evo-2 in baseline reproduction, sensitivity of results to fixed window length and rendering settings) are not discussed in the main text as limitations of the evaluation.

strengths: Genuinely original reframing: casting genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding over rendered DNA pages is a novel and thought-provoking paradigm shift, clearly articulated (Section 2.2, Appendix B distinguishes computational structure from biological structure).

Extensive and unusually thorough evaluation: three benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH eQTL, RiceSubBench, RiceWGPB), ablations vs. the DeepSeek-OCR backbone, 1D-vs-2D controlled comparisons (Appendix A), rendering/layout robustness, token bottleneck analysis, Grad-CAM interpretability, and a strict contamination analysis with k-mer containment justification (Appendix I).

The matched-token-budget, shared-backbone experiment (Table S5: 2D document 0.626 vs 1D sequence 0.558) is a well-designed control that partially isolates the representation effect from backbone and compression differences.

Comprehensive appendix coverage of prompts, task protocols, hyperparameters, and reproduction details (Evo-2/LucaOne baselines) supports reproducibility; pretraining fairness is addressed via cross-species transfer controls (Appendix O) showing OpticalDNA-HG38 outperforms HG38-pretrained sequence baselines on rice tasks.
Strong headline empirical results: 0.867 average AUROC on nine eQTL tasks with a lightweight probe, consistent gains over JanusDNA, NT-v2, GENERator, and OOD robustness on rice subspecies.
weaknesses: The efficiency narrative is partially undermined by the paper's own analysis: the '20× fewer effective tokens' claim is a token-count metric, but Table S36 shows OpticalDNA's MFLOPs/base (177.76) is far above JanusDNA (17.95) and comparable to NT-v2-500M, so actual compute savings over the strongest baselines are not demonstrated; inference throughput (0.12 M bases/s) is also modest.

Confounded comparisons: OpticalDNA inherits a large, heavily pretrained vision-language backbone (DeepSeek-OCR decoder with 570M activated parameters plus a SAM-Conv-CLIP visual front-end), whereas DNA baselines are small models trained from scratch; the '985× fewer activated parameters' framing highlights the probe size while omitting the backbone and the substantial pretraining investment (8×H100 for ~11 days on HG38 plus a second rice run). No control with a 1D DNA model pretrained at comparable compute/data scale is provided.

OCR-style capability results are mixed: masked completion (T4) achieves only ~0.13 exact match with CER ~0.58, and chromosome classification (T6) accuracy is 0.062–0.104, barely above chance (1/25), suggesting the representation captures much less genomic structure than the narrative implies.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are single runs with no confidence intervals or seed variance, yet several claimed gains are small (e.g., ablation improvements of 0.55% on CCF/WB; RiceWGPB RMSE differences of ~0.1 g between OpticalDNA and Evo-2).

RiceWGPB is scientifically questionable: predicting organism-level traits (102–130 genomes) from raw whole-genome sequence with deep learning is confounded by population structure and relatedness; the accession-level split with such tiny N cannot rule out leakage through related accessions, and no population-structure-aware baseline (e.g., GWAS/kinship-based prediction) is compared.

The 'first' claim oversells novelty: representing DNA sequences as 2D images for CNN classification has prior literature, and the pretraining tasks T4/T6 are essentially weak versions of established objectives; the OCR framing is novel but the underlying components (rendering + VLM fine-tuning + LoRA) are standard.

Full-length transcription fidelity degrades (EM 79.6%, CS 90.7% at 100% length on HG38; EM 42.3% near single-page capacity on rice), raising doubts about the 'high-fidelity compression' claim at scale.

strengths: The paper is unusually thorough in its supporting material: controlled comparisons (1D vs. 2D CNNs, matched token budgets, 1D transformers), contamination and k-mer containment analyses, rendering/layout ablations, token bottleneck experiments, and cross-species transfer controls are all present and documented in detail.

The controlled matched-token-budget experiment (Table S5, 0.626 vs. 0.558 under a shared Transformer backbone) does provide some evidence that the 2D document representation itself contributes beyond backbone or compression effects.
The task suite (T1–T6) is well specified, with formal instruction–response protocols and metric definitions (Appendices D–K) that support reproducibility.

The downstream results on DNALONGBENCH, RiceSubBench, and RiceWGPB with modest probe sizes (256K–2.3M parameters) are empirically strong relative to the compared baselines, and the impact statement addresses genomic data governance.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not convincingly established. The headline gains (0.852 AUROC vs. ~0.78 for baselines) contrast sharply with the controlled same-backbone result of 0.626 (Table S5), suggesting most of the advantage comes from transferring DeepSeek-OCR's heavily pretrained vision–language backbone rather than from the OCR-style representation itself. The paper's framing attributes the gains to the visual reformulation, but no experiment cleanly separates this from backbone pretraining quality.

The efficiency narrative is selective and partly contradicted by the paper's own data. Table S36 reports 177.76 MFLOPs/base for OpticalDNA versus 27.27 for Caduceus and 17.95 for JanusDNA; the model is among the least compute-efficient per base despite the 'understanding-driven compression' framing. The '20× fewer effective tokens' claim is not matched by end-to-end efficiency.

The 'high-fidelity, reconstructible compression' claim is not supported: full-length transcription EM drops to ~74.9–79.6% (Table 5), and many pretraining primitives largely fail — masked completion EM ≈ 0.13 (Table S32), subsequence grounding collapses under strict thresholds (Det-Acc ≈ 0.005–0.06 on HG38, Table S31), and chromosome classification is near chance (6.2–10.4%, Table S34). This undercuts the claim that OCR-style primitives naturally align with genomic operations.

Baseline comparability is questionable. NT-v2-500M and GENERator-1.2B are evaluated with frozen backbones, chunked inputs, and linear probes, which is likely a weakened configuration relative to their intended use; the 985× parameter comparison mixes activated-parameter counts across heterogeneous adaptation protocols.

The biological motivation is weak and largely conceded by the authors themselves (Appendix B): rendering a 1D sequence into a 2D monospace raster introduces artificial line breaks and spatial artifacts with no biological grounding, and a CNN over such a raster is nearly equivalent to a 1D CNN with boundary artifacts. The 'rethinking genomic modeling' framing oversells what is, by the authors' own account, a computational interface change.

Downstream feature extraction mean-pools across pages and flattens tokens into a fixed embedding, which plausibly discards exactly the long-range positional structure the method claims to preserve; the paper does not analyze whether long-range dependencies are actually captured.

The 'first vision-based DNA foundation model' claim is overstated; image-based or visual representations of sequences have been explored previously, and the related-work section does not adequately survey or distinguish from that line of work.

strengths: Highly original reframing: casting genomic modeling as OCR-style document understanding is a genuinely new paradigm, and the paper is careful to justify it as a computational (not biological) reformulation (Appendix B), which strengthens the conceptual contribution.

The controlled comparisons in Appendix A are unusually thorough for a foundation-model paper: matched token budget with a shared Transformer backbone (Table S5, +12.2% relative for the 2D representation), comparisons against 1D CNNs, RNNs, linear/sparse attention, and 1D Transformers — this does real work isolating the representation effect from backbone and compression confounds.

Empirical results are broad and mostly convincing: SOTA on DNALONG eQTL (0.852/0.867 AUROC with 256K–2.3M trainable params), consistent OOD gains on rice subspecies, best RMSE on whole-genome phenotype prediction, and cross-species transfer from HG38 to rice that rules out domain-matched pretraining as the sole explanation (Table S39).

Extensive ablations beyond the headline results: token bottleneck analysis, rendering/layout/font robustness, resolution sensitivity, Grad-CAM interpretability with page-level attribution, and strict contamination analyses (full-sequence overlap plus a well-designed 20-mer containment/label-consistency analysis in Table S26).
Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameter tables for two-stage HG38 and rice pretraining, downstream search spaces, baseline reproduction details for Evo-2/LucaOne, and a code link.
Honest treatment of weak spots: T6 chromosome classification (0.062 acc), T4 masked completion (EM ~0.13), and T5 grounding bottlenecks are reported transparently with discussion rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Fairness of some headline comparisons is questionable. The '985× fewer activated parameters' framing compares against a frozen Enformer, while OpticalDA itself sits on top of a heavily pretrained DeepSeek-OCR stack (SAM-Conv-CLIP-L vision front-end + 3B MoE decoder, 570M activated) pretrained on natural documents — the gains may partly reflect general vision-language pretraining rather than the OCR-on-DNA paradigm per se. A from-scratch or DNA-randomly-initialized ablation of the backbone would strengthen the claim.

Margins on the primary human benchmark over the strongest baseline are modest (0.867 vs 0.840 AUROC for JanusDNA MLP), and several baselines (NT-v2-500M, GENERator-1.2B) are evaluated with chunking + linear probes that may under-tune them; no variance/statistical significance is reported.

RiceWGPB has very small sample sizes (102 and 130 total samples; 21/26 test), making RMSE differences (e.g., 2.952 vs 3.056 for Evo-2) potentially within noise; no confidence intervals are provided, and Evo-2/LucaOne comparisons use frozen features + linear heads that may disadvantage them.

The 'understanding-driven compression' narrative is not directly validated: measured compression is only ~19–21×, and transcription fidelity degrades near single-page capacity (EM 42.3% at 1792–2048 bp, Table S28), raising questions about fine-grained information retention at longer spans.

Some pretraining task results are weak (T4 completion, T6 classification near chance), so the claimed six-primitive capability suite overstates current capability; the paper acknowledges this but the abstract does not.

Scientific explanation for why rasterized 2D rendering beats 1D remains largely correlational; the mechanism (region-aware inductive bias, selective computation) is plausible but not probed with e.g. attention/locus-level analyses on the eQTL tasks themselves.
